section_summary: This section continues a historical study of Japanese society, tracing the assimilation of Chinese culture and Buddhism during the Nara and Heian periods and the emergence of military feudalism under the Kamakura and Ashikaga regimes. It then examines Tokugawa efforts to stabilize society through seclusion, rigid class distinctions, and regulation, emphasizing the economic decline of the daimyo and samurai, the oppression of cultivators, and the growing influence of merchants. Literary, religious, and artistic examples—including court literature, warrior tales, Buddhism, tea culture, Kabuki, Noh, prints, and poetry—illustrate changes in Japanese ideals and everyday life.

subfiles.title: Historical Survey of Japanese Society and Feudalism, chapters 2–4 (continuation)
subfiles.about: A historical and sociological account of Japanese cultural development, military feudalism, Tokugawa seclusion, class relations, economic change, religion, literature, and the arts.
subfiles.summary: The continuation first considers Chinese writing, Confucianism, Buddhism, literature, and art in the Nara and Heian periods, contrasting refined court culture with weakening government, economic strain, and the emergence of hereditary warriors. It then traces the establishment of the Kamakura shogunate, the growth of feudal loyalties and household authority, the Ashikaga disorders, and the unification policies of Nobunaga, Hideyoshi, and Ieyasu. The discussion of the Tokugawa period emphasizes political seclusion, rigid social regulation, daimyo and samurai indebtedness, peasant oppression, the rise of a money economy, and the prosperity of urban merchants. Examples from chronicles, novels, drama, painting, and poetry illustrate the changing ideals and emotional life of different social classes.
